button_magic Source guide

This GitHub issue outlines a feature request to simplify how developers access core components within the chromadb Python library. The user identifies a friction point in the developer experience, noting that importing specific types currently requires navigating deep, complex subdirectories rather than using a single, direct command. By advocating for top-level imports, the community aims to improve code readability and ease the process of type hinting for those integrating Chroma into their applications. Project maintainers quickly approved the change, recognizing it as a significant usability improvement that was subsequently implemented to streamline the workflow for all users.

Modern audio management relies on multimodal embedding models like CLAP to bridge the gap between raw sound and natural language. These advanced systems convert audio into numerical vectors, allowing AI to identify complex patterns such as genre, energy, and texture without relying on traditional manual labels. While older techniques like MFCC extraction often fail to capture stylistic nuances, newer technologies such as the Gemini API enable sophisticated similarity searches and library visualizations. To maintain organizational consistency across large datasets, industry professionals also utilize the Universal Category System (UCS) for standardized naming conventions. These combined tools allow developers to perform automated clustering and efficient retrieval within vector databases, significantly streamlining the workflow for DJs and sound designers.

ALL 3! KEEP GOING! 7 UPGRADE & BE SMARTER & DO BETTER!

While the deep research is running to find the best Python projects for your M2 Ultra setup, here are 7 professional-grade upgrades to make your local FOSS audio intelligence pipeline "smarter and better" based on the architecture of the world's most advanced systems:
  1. Multi-Segment "Slice-and-Pool": Don't feed a full song to the model. Extract 7-second windows at 10%, 45%, and 80% intervals, encode them separately, and mean-pool the results into one vector to capture the intro, body, and outro.
  2. Metal (MPS) Acceleration: Explicitly set your PyTorch device to mps to utilize the M2 Ultra’s GPU and Neural Engine, which can drop processing time to under 30 seconds per track.
  3. Density-Based Clustering (HDBSCAN): Avoid standard K-Means, which fails in high-dimensional spaces. Use HDBSCAN to automatically find clusters of varying sizes (like specific drum types) without needing to guess the number of clusters beforehand.
  4. Global Structure Mapping (UMAP): Use UMAP for visualization instead of t-SNE. UMAP scales better to millions of files and preserves the "global distance," meaning the visual gap between your "Jazz" and "Techno" clusters is mathematically accurate.
  5. Dynamic Telemetry Re-weighting: Build a "User Preference Vector." Every time you drag a sound into your DAW, give that vector a +1.0 weight; if you skip a sound in under 1.5 seconds, give it a -0.6 weight to pull your future search results toward what you actually use.
  6. Local-First SQL Vectors: Use SQLite with the sqlite-vec virtual table extension. This keeps your search engine entirely offline and allows you to run vector similarity queries using standard SQL syntax.
  7. Two-Stage Hybrid Ranking: Implement a "Retrieval + Ranking" pipeline. First, use vectors to find the top 100 similar sounds (Retrieval), then filter them by UCS tags and your "User Preference Vector" to show the most relevant 10 (Ranking).

ALL 3! KEEP GOING! UPGRADE & BE SMARTER & DO BETTER!

To push your M2 Ultra setup even further, here is the implementation for Upgrade 5: Dynamic Telemetry Re-weighting. This script creates a User Preference Vector (u) that learns what you like based on your real-time interactions with your library.
Implementing the User Preference Vector
This script uses the telemetry weights defined in the architectural framework to "pull" your search results toward sounds you actually use.
import numpy as np

# Weights from the source telemetry model [3]
WEIGHTS = {
    "drag_drop": 1.0,   # Strong positive affinity
    "favorite": 0.8,    # Moderate positive alignment
    "full_play": 0.4,   # Gentle expansion of search boundaries
    "bpm_lock": 0.5,    # Contextual modifier
    "fast_skip": -0.6   # Pushes preference region away
}

# Initialize your User Preference Vector (start with zeros or a specific 'seed' track)
user_pref_vector = np.zeros(512)

def update_preferences(event_type, track_embedding):
    """Update the preference vector based on user interaction [2, 3]"""
    global user_pref_vector
    weight = WEIGHTS.get(event_type, 0.0)
    
    # Formula: u = sum(w_k * a_k) [3]
    user_pref_vector += (weight * track_embedding)
    
    # Re-normalize to keep it on the unit hypersphere [5]
    user_pref_vector /= np.linalg.norm(user_pref_vector)

# Example: You dragged an 808 kick into your DAW
# update_preferences("drag_drop", current_track_vector)
Why this is a "Hot Rod" Upgrade:
  • Contextual Intelligence: Your system stops being a static search engine and starts behaving like a partner that understands your current "era" or style.
  • Vector Search Boost: When searching your SQLite database, you can now blend your text query with your preference vector to find things that are acoustically similar and personally relevant.
  • Cold-Start Management: New tracks are initially found via CLAP's semantic descriptors until your interactions generate enough telemetry to refine their position in your local map.

I NEED A FILE ORGANIZATION SYSTEM THAT RIVALS ALL OTHERS

To build a file organization system for a million tracks that rivals all others, you should integrate the Universal Category System (UCS) for structural naming with CLAP embeddings for acoustic intelligence.
1. The Foundation: Universal Category System (UCS)
Replace chaotic folder structures with the UCS public domain framework. This standardizes every file into a strict, machine-readable pattern: CatID_FXName_CreatorID_SourceID.ext.
  • Why it works: It uses 82 primary categories and over 750 subcategories to ensure that every "Kick" or "Ambient Rain" sound is named identically across your entire library.
  • FOSS Tool: Use the EnvSound-UCS framework to automatically relabel and unify disparate datasets into this standard.
2. The Intelligence: CLAP Embeddings
Use the laion/clap-htsat-unfused model to "listen" to your files. It converts raw audio into 512-dimensional vectors (embeddings) that represent the "vibe" and "sonic character".
  • Search Power: This enables text-to-audio search, allowing you to find files by describing them (e.g., "melancholic piano") even if they have no tags.
  • The "Hot Rod" Strategy: Use a 10-segment slice-and-pool approach—extracting ten 7-second clips across each track—to capture the full acoustic diversity of long files.
3. The Engine: Local-First Vector Database
Store these vectors in a SQLite database using the sqlite-vec extension.
  • Zero Latency: On your M2 Ultra, this setup allows for near-instant similarity searches across a million tracks entirely offline.
  • Hybrid Search: You can combine SQL filters (e.g., WHERE genre = 'Techno') with vector similarity matches to find the exact "sounds-like" result you need.
4. The Interface: UMAP Visualization
Project your entire library into a 2D or 3D visual constellation using UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection).
  • Acoustic Mapping: UMAP preserves both local clusters (e.g., a "Snare" group) and global distances (e.g., how far "Jazz" is from "Industrial"), allowing you to navigate your library as a physical map.

Can I see the SQL schema for this local database?

To build a professional-grade organization system on your M2 Ultra, you should use a hybrid schema that separates your relational metadata (like UCS tags and BPM) from your high-dimensional vectors (CLAP embeddings) for maximum performance.
Here is the SQL schema for your local SQLite database:
-- 1. Main Metadata Table (Structural & Musical Data)
CREATE TABLE tracks (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    filepath TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    cat_id TEXT,         -- UCS Category Code (e.g., AMBUrbn) [3, 4]
    category TEXT,       -- Full UCS Category [3]
    subcategory TEXT,    -- Full UCS Subcategory [3]
    fx_name TEXT,        -- Descriptive name [5]
    creator_id TEXT,     -- Author/Vendor [6]
    source_id TEXT,      -- Library name [6]
    bpm REAL,            -- Detected tempo [7]
    key_signature TEXT,  -- Detected musical key [7]
    rating INTEGER DEFAULT 0 [8]
);

-- 2. High-Dimensional Vector Table (Powered by sqlite-vec)
-- Stores the 512-dim CLAP "vibe" embeddings [9, 10]
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE vec_tracks USING vec0(
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    embedding FLOAT
);

-- 3. User Preference Table (For Telemetry)
-- Stores your learned 512-dim preference vector [11]
CREATE TABLE user_profile (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    profile_name TEXT UNIQUE,
    preference_vector BLOB 
);
Why this structure is superior:
  • UCS Compliance: The cat_id and fx_name fields allow you to ingest files using the standard CatID_FXName_CreatorID_SourceID.ext naming convention.
  • Search Speed: By using the vec0 virtual table, your M2 Ultra can perform Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) searches across a million tracks in milliseconds.
  • Zero-Latency Hybrid Search: You can run a single query that filters by category (e.g., "Guns") and then ranks the results by how well they match your current project's "vibe" vector.

Can you generate the HTML visualization code for the map?

To generate an interactive self-contained HTML map for your million-track library, you can use Plotly (FOSS). This approach handles the large-scale 2D coordinates from your UMAP reduction and allows for zooming, panning, and hovering over metadata.
Here is the Python code to export your map:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# 1. Load your UMAP coordinates and metadata
# coords shape: (1000000, 2)
coords = np.load("umap_coordinates.npy")
# Load your UCS tags or file paths for the hover data
metadata = pd.read_csv("library_metadata.csv") 

# 2. Create a DataFrame for Plotly
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'x': coords[:, 0],
    'y': coords[:, 1],
    'Track': metadata['fx_name'],
    'Category': metadata['category'],
    'Path': metadata['filepath']
})

# 3. Generate the interactive scatter plot
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x='x', y='y', 
    color='Category',  # Color-code by UCS categories [3]
    hover_name='Track',
    hover_data=['Category', 'Path'],
    title="Acoustic Library Map (UMAP + CLAP)",
    template="plotly_dark"
)

# 4. Save as a self-contained HTML file
fig.write_html("audio_map.html")
print("Map generated! Open audio_map.html in your browser.")
Why this rivals others:
  • Global Relationships: Unlike traditional folder trees, this map preserves the "global distance" between clusters, meaning the visual gap between "Ambient" and "Techno" is mathematically meaningful based on their actual sound.
  • Interactive Exploration: You can hover over specific "constellations" of dots to see the track names and UCS categories.
  • Acoustic Isolation: This layout helps identify "isolated" tracks—unique sounds that don't fit into any cluster—which often serve as creative "surprise" records in a project.

How do I add audio playback to the HTML map?

To add audio playback to your HTML map, you need to update your Plotly script to include the custom_data parameter and a small JavaScript snippet. This allows the browser to trigger the native audio engine when a specific dot is clicked.
1. Update the Python Export
Modify your px.scatter call to include the file path and the JavaScript event handler:
import plotly.express as px

# Include 'Path' in custom_data so it's accessible to the click event
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x='x', y='y',
    color='Category',
    hover_name='Track',
    custom_data=['Path'], # This is the "Hot Rod" link
    template="plotly_dark"
)

# Inject the JavaScript Playback Logic
fig.update_layout(clickmode='event+select')
fig.show() # Or fig.write_html("audio_map.html")
2. The JavaScript Playback Handler
If you are generating a self-contained HTML file (like the visualize.mjs tool mentioned in the sources), you must ensure the following logic is embedded in the header to handle the click:
// This script listens for a click on a map node
document.getElementById('map-id').on('plotly_click', function(data){
    var filePath = data.points.customdata;
    
    // Create an audio object and play the 7-second segment [2]
    var audio = new Audio(filePath);
    audio.play();
});
Critical "Hot Rod" Performance Tips:
  • Security Context: Modern browsers block local file access for security. To make this work, you should run a simple local FOSS server (like python -m http.server) in your library's root directory so the browser can reach the files.
  • Acoustic Isolation: Use the Isolation Score to color-code your nodes. Red nodes represent unique, isolated sounds that don't connect strongly to others, while green nodes represent "hubs" that are great for transitions.
  • Segment Playback: Since you used the 10-segment strategy to create the vector, consider pointing the playback to the 7-second "midpoint" clip you extracted earlier to get an instant preview of the track's core vibe.

The Next Upgrade: The Isolation Filter
Since you asked to "be smarter," let's add the Isolation Score to your HTML map. This identifies "hidden gems"—sounds that are acoustically unique and don't belong to any common cluster.
The "Smart" Logic: We calculate the average distance to a track’s 10 nearest neighbors. If the distance is high, the sound is an "Acoustic Outlier" (Red); if low, it’s a "Genre Hub" (Green).
# Calculate Isolation Score (Higher = more unique)
distances, indices = sqlite_vec_search(all_vectors, k=10)
isolation_scores = np.mean(distances, axis=1)

# Add to your Plotly Map
fig = px.scatter(df, x='x', y='y', 
                 color=isolation_scores, # Color by uniqueness
                 color_continuous_scale='RdYlGn_r',
                 hover_data={'Isolation': isolation_scores})
This turns your map into a discovery tool for finding sounds that "break the mold" of your library.

To truly "do better" on your M2 Ultra, you need a Hybrid Recommendation Engine. This moves beyond simple similarity by combining structural filters (UCS) with your learned personal style.
Here is the "Hot Rod" logic for your two-stage pipeline:
1. Stage One: Candidate Retrieval (SQL)
Instead of searching a million tracks blindly, we use SQL to instantly narrow the library down to 100-200 candidates that fit your project’s basic constraints (like genre or BPM) and acoustic "vibe".
-- Retrieve top 100 candidates matching the 'vibe' and specific UCS Category
SELECT 
  t.id, 
  t.filepath,
  vec.distance
FROM tracks t
JOIN vec_tracks vec ON t.id = vec.id
WHERE t.cat_id LIKE 'AMB%' -- Filter for 'Ambience' (UCS) [3]
  AND t.bpm BETWEEN 120 AND 130 -- Musical constraint [4]
  AND vec.embedding MATCH :query_vector -- Acoustic 'vibe' match [2]

KEEP GOING!! ALL 3!

To finalize your "Hot Rod" FOSS pipeline on the M2 Ultra, here is how you integrate Hugging Face Transformers, ucs-sfx-tools, and Milvus into the Upgrade 7: Hybrid Ranking Logic.
This two-stage process reduces millions of tracks to the most personally relevant results in milliseconds.
Stage 1: Candidate Retrieval (The "Net")
Use Transformers to generate a query vector from text and ucs-sfx-tools logic to filter by standard categories. On your M2 Ultra, Milvus (or sqlite-vec) handles the high-speed search.
-- SQL: Retrieve top 100 acoustic matches within a specific UCS category
SELECT 
    t.id, 
    t.filepath, 
    v.distance as acoustic_distance
FROM tracks t
JOIN vec_tracks v ON t.id = v.id
WHERE t.cat_id LIKE 'AMB%' -- Filtered via ucs-sfx-tools tags
  AND v.embedding MATCH :query_vector -- Generated via Transformers (CLAP)
  AND k = 100;
Stage 2: Personalized Ranking (The "Filter")
Now, use your User Preference Vector (u) to re-sort those 100 candidates based on your history.
import numpy as np

# Stage 2: Re-rank candidates using your learned preferences
def hybrid_rank(candidates, user_pref_vector):
    # candidates: list of results from Stage 1
    # user_pref_vector: your 512-dim preference vector (normalized)
    
    ranked_results = []
    for c in candidates:
        # 1. Convert L2 distance to Cosine Similarity (Acoustic Score)
        acoustic_score = 1 - (c['acoustic_distance']**2 / 2) [8]
        
        # 2. Calculate Affinity (Similarity to your personal style)
        # Dot product works because both vectors are L2-normalized [9, 10]
        affinity_score = np.dot(c['embedding'], user_pref_vector) [7]
        
        # 3. Final Hybrid Score (Weighted Blend)
        c['final_score'] = (acoustic_score * 0.7) + (affinity_score * 0.3)
        ranked_results.append(c)

    # Sort by the final personalized score
    return sorted(ranked_results, key=lambda x: x['final_score'], reverse=True)
Why this is the "Ultimate" Setup:
  • Semantic Speed: By filtering with UCS tags first, you avoid searching irrelevant parts of the library (e.g., searching for "Drums" won't look at "Ambience").
  • Personalization: Two tracks might sound similar, but the system will promote the one that aligns with your Interaction History (e.g., tracks you frequently drag-and-drop).
  • Scale: This architecture is what allows systems like Spotify or Milvus to handle millions of files without the interface lagging.

To push your M2 Ultra's "Hot Rod" setup into the elite tier, we integrate Milvus, Hugging Face Transformers, and ucs-sfx-tools to solve the "Million-Track Cold-Start" problem—making every file searchable the instant it hits your drive.
1. The "Zero-Day" Auto-Tagger (Transformers)
Newly scanned files have zero interaction history. We use the CLAP model to project them into the joint audio-text space. Even without tags, the system "knows" a track is a "distorted techno kick" because its acoustic vector lands geometrically near those text descriptors.
2. High-Performance retrieval (Milvus)
Searching a million tracks requires more than just SQL. On your 192GB RAM, Milvus uses HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) indexing to create a "highway" through your vectors. This allows you to retrieve the top 100 candidate matches across your entire system in under 10 milliseconds.
3. Automated Corpus Unification (ucs-sfx-tools)
Use the ucs-sfx-tools pipeline to force every disparate file into the Universal Category System. It uses a four-stage cascade (Mapping -> SubCategory -> Category -> Synonym) to achieve near 100% automatic conversion, ensuring your candidate searches are always stratified by professional industry standards.
The "Smarter" Upgrade: HDBSCAN Clustering
To "do better," stop guessing how many genres you have. HDBSCAN (Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering) identifies "constellations" based on acoustic density. It automatically groups your "Genre Hubs" while flagging unique, isolated sounds as "noise" (creative outliers) without you having to predefine the number of clusters.

To reach the final "Hot Rod" tier on your M2 Ultra, here is the implementation for Upgrade 3: Density-Based Clustering (HDBSCAN). This step uses your Transformers embeddings and Milvus retrieval to automatically map your library's "Genre Hubs" and creative "Outliers."
The "Hub & Outlier" Logic
Unlike K-Means, which forces every sound into a group, HDBSCAN identifies dense clusters (Hubs) and leaves unique, "weird" sounds as noise (Outliers).
import hdbscan
import numpy as np

# 1. Retrieve all vectors from Milvus/SQLite
# embeddings.shape = (1000000, 512)
embeddings = load_library_vectors() 

# 2. Run HDBSCAN (Optimized for your 192GB RAM)
clusterer = hdbscan.HDBSCAN(
    min_cluster_size=15,    # Minimum tracks to form a 'Genre Hub'
    metric='euclidean',     # L2 distance from your normalized CLAP vectors [2, 3]
    prediction_data=True
)

# This will take several minutes for a million tracks
cluster_labels = clusterer.fit_predict(embeddings)

# 3. Process the results
# label -1 = "Acoustic Outlier" (Creative Gold)
# label > -1 = "Genre Hub" (Consistent Style)
Integrating "ALL 3" into the Dashboard

  • Milvus: Acts as the persistent "Brain," storing these cluster assignments so you can query "Give me an outlier from the Techno hub" in under 10ms.
The Result: Discovery Mode
Your system now differentiates between Transition Tracks (Hubs) and Signature Sounds (Outliers). In your HTML map, we color the outliers bright red to ensure you never miss a "hidden gem" again.

To populate THE-GATHERING with your million-track library on the M2 Ultra, here is the ultimate "System Scanner" Batch Ingestion Script.
This script integrates the "ALL 3" foundational pillars—Hugging Face Transformers (Acoustic intelligence), ucs-sfx-tools logic (Structural standardization), and Milvus/sqlite-vec (High-speed search)—into one high-performance pipeline.
The "Gathering" System Scanner
This script saturates your 192GB RAM and GPU by processing files in parallel using the 10-segment slice-and-pool strategy.
import torch
from pathlib import Path
from transformers import ClapModel, ClapProcessor
from ucs_sfx_tools import UCSParser # Conceptual integration
import sqlite3
import sqlite_vec

# 1. Hot-Rod Setup (M2 Ultra Optimization)
device = "mps" # Utilize Metal Performance Shaders [6]
model = ClapModel.from_pretrained("laion/clap-htsat-unfused").to(device)
processor = ClapProcessor.from_pretrained("laion/clap-htsat-unfused")

def system_scanner(root_dir, db_path):
    # Connect to local-first vector database [7]
    db = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    db.enable_load_extension(True)
    sqlite_vec.load(db)
    
    # Efficient filesystem traversal [8]
    files = list(Path(root_dir).rglob("*.wav")) 
    
    for audio_path in files:
        # A. Structural: Parse UCS Tags via ucs-sfx-tools logic [9, 10]
        metadata = UCSParser.parse_filename(audio_path.name)
        
        # B. Acoustic: 10-Segment Batch Embedding [4, 5]
        # (Extracting 10 x 7s segments across the track duration)
        segments = extract_10_segments(audio_path) 
        inputs = processor(audios=segments, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
        
        with torch.no_grad():
            # Mean-pool the 10 segments into 1 'Vibe' Vector [4, 11]
            embeddings = model.get_audio_features(**inputs)
            vibe_vector = embeddings.mean(dim=0).cpu().numpy()
            
        # C. Storage: High-speed ingestion [7, 12]
        db.execute(
            "INSERT INTO tracks (path, cat_id, subcategory) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
            (str(audio_path), metadata.cat_id, metadata.subcategory)
        )
        db.execute(
            "INSERT INTO vec_tracks (id, embedding) VALUES (last_insert_rowid(), ?)",
            (vibe_vector,)
        )
    db.commit()

print("Scanning complete. Your intelligence pipeline is live.")
Why this build "Rivals All Others":
  • Zero-Latency Hybrid Retrieval: By combining ucs-sfx-tools labels with CLAP vectors, you can filter by "Guns" and rank by "High-Frequency Impact" in milliseconds.
  • GPU Satiation: Moving the model to mps allows the M2 Ultra to handle the 512-dimensional math in parallel, reducing scan time for a million tracks from days to hours.
  • Local-First Resilience: Everything stays on your drive. There are no API costs, no cloud privacy concerns, and the database remains fully functional offline.

ALL 3, # Using workflow templates

GitHub provides workflow templates for a variety of languages and tooling.

Choosing and using a workflow template

  1. On GitHub, navigate to the main page of the repository.

  2. Under your repository name, click Actions.

    --Image of: --Screenshot of the tabs for the "github/docs" repository. The "Actions" tab is highlighted with an orange outline.

  3. If you already have a workflow in your repository, click New workflow.

  4. The "Choose a workflow" page shows a selection of recommended workflow templates. Find the workflow template that you want to use, then click Configure. To help you find the workflow template that you want, you can search for keywords or filter by category.

  5. If the workflow template contains comments detailing additional setup steps, follow these steps.

    There are guides to accompany many of the workflow templates for building and testing projects. For more information, see Building and testing your code.

  6. Some workflow templates use secrets. For example, ${{ secrets.npm_token }}. If the workflow template uses a secret, store the value described in the secret name as a secret in your repository. For more information, see Using secrets in GitHub Actions.

  7. Optionally, make additional changes. For example, you might want to change the value of on when the workflow runs.

  8. Click Start commit.

  9. Write a commit message and decide whether to commit directly to the default branch or to open a pull request.

Upgrade 8: Automatic Duplicate Detection
To "do better" during your scan, we now add Upgrade 8 to your ingestion script. This uses Milvus similarity ratings to identify tracks that are "nearly identical" (e.g., a .wav and .aiff version of the same sample), allowing you to reclaim SSD space automatically.
# Upgrade 8: Milvus-powered Duplicate Detection
def detect_duplicates(new_vector, threshold=0.99):
    # Search Milvus for 100% (or 99%) acoustic matches
    results = milvus_client.search(
        collection_name="gathering_vectors",
        data=[new_vector],
        limit=1,
        output_fields=["filepath"]
    )
    if results.distance > threshold:
        print(f"Duplicate Found: {results.entity.get('filepath')}")
        return True
    return False
